theme: Clean and unclean; skin diseases, holiness as separation
readingInstruction: Read Leviticus 11:1-13:59. These chapters are some of the strangest in the Bible. They describe clean and unclean animals, childbirth, and skin diseases. Read them with one question in mind: what is God teaching his people about holiness?
settingTheScene: After the ordination of the priests and the offerings, Leviticus turns to the question of what is clean and unclean. The Hebrew words are tameh and tahor. “Unclean” does not mean “sinful” or “dirty.” It means unfit for the sanctuary. The laws apply to food, to childbirth, to skin diseases, and to mildew in clothing. They govern daily life, and they remind Israel at every meal and every household event that they are a people set apart.
observation: The land animals that may be eaten are those that chew the cud and have a split hoof (11:1-8).
Water creatures with fins and scales are allowed, and other sea creatures are not (11:9-12).
Many birds and insects are named as unclean (11:13-23).
“For I am the LORD who brought you up out of the land of Egypt to be your God. You shall therefore be holy, for I am holy” (11:45).
After childbirth, a mother is unclean for a period, and then brings a burnt offering and a sin offering (12:1-8).
The priest examines skin conditions and declares a person clean or unclean (13:1-46).
The one who is unclean must “live alone. His dwelling shall be outside the camp” (13:46).
The same rules apply to mildew in clothing (13:47-59).
interpretation:
Why does God give these laws? The Bible does not give one simple answer, but the text points to several truths.

The first is explicit: the laws teach holiness. Leviticus 11:44-45 says, “For I am the LORD your God. Consecrate yourselves, and be holy, for I am holy.” The food laws are one way that Israel’s daily life is shaped by the idea of separation. At every meal, an Israelite was reminded that he belonged to a God who had set his people apart from the nations. These laws marked the boundary between Israel and the world.

The second is that they teach us to distinguish. The categories of clean and unclean train the people to think about the difference between what belongs in God’s presence and what does not. Many of the unclean things are associated with death, decay, or disorder. The uncleanness of skin disease and discharge points to the brokenness of a world under death. These conditions were not sins, but they were signs of a fallen creation, and so they kept a person out of the sanctuary.

Third, the exclusion of the unclean person from the camp is a sobering picture. The person with a serious skin disease had to live alone, tear his clothes, and cry, “Unclean, unclean.” It is one of the loneliest images in the Bible. It shows what sin and death do: they separate us from the community and from God’s presence.

But note the role of the priest. He does not cause the uncleanness. He examines and pronounces. And as chapter 14 will show, the priest is also the one who declares a cleansed person clean. The system points to a need that it cannot meet. It shows that people cannot cleanse themselves.

We should be careful about using these laws for health advice, or for ranking people. They belong to Israel’s life under the old covenant, and the New Testament tells us that their purpose has been fulfilled. In Mark 7:19, Jesus declares all foods clean. In Acts 10, Peter is told, “What God has made clean, do not call common.”
connection: Jesus touched lepers and healed them (Mark 1:40-42), and instead of being made unclean, he made them clean. Paul says that “nothing is unclean in itself” (Romans 14:14), and that in Christ the dividing wall between Jew and Gentile has been broken down (Ephesians 2:14). Hebrews 13:12 says that Jesus suffered outside the gate, in the place of the unclean. Peter’s vision in Acts 10 shows the end of the food distinction as a mark of God’s people.
application:
Think about the call to be holy and set apart. What areas of life show that you belong to God?

Remember someone who is isolated by illness, shame, or circumstance. Ask how you could reach out to them in the way that Jesus reached out to the lepers.

Thank God that in Christ, what was unclean is made clean, and that the barrier is gone.
prayerPrompts: Ask God to make you holy in a way that draws people to him.
Thank Jesus for touching the unclean and making them clean.
Ask him to show you someone who is alone and how you might reach them.
